power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Open data can extend the use of participants' information far beyond the study for which it was collected, making informed consent for data sharing an important part of research transparency.
We examined whether psychology journals that promote open data address this issue in their guidelines and whether articles sharing data report relevant information about consent.
We reviewed the websites of 83 journals identified through the TOP Factor list and examined 196 empirical articles sharing data, published in 2024-2025.

No journal provided explicit guidance on obtaining consent specifically for sharing participants' data on open platforms; four required authors to report consent for secondary data use when applicable.
Only seven articles (3.57%) provided information connecting informed consent to data sharing, and in six cases this information was identifiable only in repository materials.
These findings reveal a transparency gap: consent for data sharing is rarely made explicit in journal guidance or research reports, even when data are openly shared.
We recommend clearer communication with participants about data sharing, more detailed reporting and sharing of consent materials, and stronger guidance from journals and institutions.
Among these initiatives, data sharing has progressively become one of the cornerstones of transparent research.

Increasingly, researchers are expected not only to publish the results of their studies, but also to make the underlying data available so that other scholars can reproduce published analyses, conduct secondary analyses, combine datasets across studies, and generate new scientific knowledge from existing data (Lindsay, 2017).
text.formatted: Increasingly, researchers are expected not only to publish the results of their studies, but also to make the underlying data available so that other scholars can reproduce published analyses, conduct secondary analyses, combine datasets across studies, and generate new scientific knowledge from existing data <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Lindsay, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Many psychology journals have subsequently adopted Open Science badges to incentivize and recognize transparent research practices.
These initiatives also institutionalize standards of good scientific practice and shape researchers' expectations and behaviors (Stodden et al., 2013).
text.formatted: These initiatives also institutionalize standards of good scientific practice and shape researchers' expectations and behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Stodden et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: One of the most important consequences of the Open Science movement, and data sharing in particular, is that it has fundamentally transformed the research data life cycle.
Traditionally, the relationship between participants and researchers largely ended once data collection was completed, and study findings were published.

Today, however, publication may instead mark the beginning of a dataset's scientific life: once deposited in a repository, data can remain available indefinitely, be accessed by new researchers, combined with other datasets, or reused to address questions not anticipated when participants agreed to participate.

Journal policies and Open Science badges have further encouraged researchers to make their data available for future use, while also drawing increasing attention to the conditions and practices needed to ensure that shared data are not merely available, but genuinely reusable in practice.
Despite this expanded data life cycle, discussions of open data have largely focused on whether datasets are available, adequately documented, and reusable (e.g., Neve & Rousselet, 2025).
text.formatted: Despite this expanded data life cycle, discussions of open data have largely focused on whether datasets are available, adequately documented, and reusable (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Neve & Rousselet, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These are important questions, but they primarily concern how researchers manage data after collection.

This emphasis risks framing research data primarily as outputs of the scientific process, products to be generated, curated, and shared, while overlooking the fact that data are first and foremost co-produced through participants' interactions with researchers, research procedures, and measurement tools.
Are participants adequately informed that at least part of their data may remain available and be reused long after the original study has ended?
Do they understand what data sharing is, why it is scientifically valuable, which of their data may be shared, and under what conditions?

In other words, while Open Science has devoted substantial effort to promoting transparency among researchers, considerably less attention has been paid to transparency toward individuals whose data make scientific openness possible.
The ethical debate surrounding open data has traditionally focused on privacy and confidentiality.

Specifically, the literature provides extensive guidance on how to remove participants' identifiers before sharing data to minimize disclosure risks, especially in research involving sensitive topics and vulnerable populations (e.g., Prosser et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Specifically, the literature provides extensive guidance on how to remove participants' identifiers before sharing data to minimize disclosure risks, especially in research involving sensitive topics and vulnerable populations (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Prosser et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, methodological effort has focused on de-identification, pseudonymization, controlled-access repositories, federated analyses, and trusted research environments (Tamuhla et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Accordingly, methodological effort has focused on de-identification, pseudonymization, controlled-access repositories, federated analyses, and trusted research environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Tamuhla et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Privacy protection is only one dimension of ethical data sharing.

Even when re-identification risks are minimized, a distinct question remains: have participants been enabled to make an informed and voluntary decision about the future circulation and reuse of their data?
Confidentiality safeguards concern how data should be protected; whereas informed consent concerns whether participants understand and authorize how their contribution may be used.
The former cannot substitute for the latter.
This distinction shifts attention from data protection alone to participant autonomy.

Traditionally, informed consent has enabled individuals to decide whether to participate in a specific study after receiving understandable information about its aims, procedures, risks, benefits and their rights.

Data sharing expands the temporal and scientific scope of this decision, as participants' data may be preserved and reused by other researchers for purposes that cannot be fully anticipated at the time of consent.

For this reason, data-sharing plans should be incorporated into research design from its earliest stages and be transparently presented to participants within the informed consent (Lindsay, 2017; Meyer, 2018).
text.formatted: For this reason, data-sharing plans should be incorporated into research design from its earliest stages and be transparently presented to participants within the informed consent <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Lindsay, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Meyer, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Empirical studies suggest that such transparency is not necessarily an obstacle to data sharing.

Participants are generally supportive of secondary scientific use of their data when it is accompanied by transparent governance, trustworthy institutions, and clear information regarding the conditions for the future uses of their data (e.g., Reeves et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Participants are generally supportive of secondary scientific use of their data when it is accompanied by transparent governance, trustworthy institutions, and clear information regarding the conditions for the future uses of their data (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Reeves et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The ethical implications of data sharing have been discussed far more extensively in biobanking, genomics, and clinical research than in psychology (Allen et al., 2013; Christofidou et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The ethical implications of data sharing have been discussed far more extensively in biobanking, genomics, and clinical research than in psychology <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Allen et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Christofidou et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In these fields, because future users, research questions, and analytical technologies cannot always be specified when data are collected, alternative approaches to traditional study-specific consent have already been developed, including broad, tiered, dynamic, and meta-consent.

All these consent models share a central premise: future data sharing should be incorporated into the informed consent process rather than treated solely as a data-management decision of the researchers after data collection.

Recent proposals in clinical research similarly recommended dedicated participantcentered consent provisions through which participants can explicitly authorize the secondary sharing of their de-identified data (Trippa & Khozin, 2024).

text.text: Against this background, psychological science appears to have devoted comparatively limited attention to how participants should be informed about, and involved in, decisions concerning the future sharing and use of their data.

This is particularly striking because psychological research frequently collects sensitive information concerning mental health, cognitive functioning, personality, traumatic experiences, and many other aspects of individuals' private lives.

Having rapidly developed repositories, reporting standards, Open Science badges, and transparency guidelines to facilitate data sharing, psychology may now be well positioned to address an equally important ethical challenge: ensuring that the expansion of open data is accompanied by equally robust practices for informing participants about, and involving them in, decisions concerning the future use of their data.
These challenges do not arise in an ethical vacuum.
Rather, they can be interpreted through ethical principles that have long governed research involving human participants.

We considered two authoritative frameworks relevant to psychological research: the American Psychological Although neither framework directly addresses many practices associated with contemporary Open Science, such as depositing data in public repositories, enabling secondary analyses by unknown future users, or preserving datasets over the long term, their principles concerning participant autonomy, transparency, informed decision-making, confidentiality, and responsible stewardship have clear implications for data sharing.
We therefore synthesized these principles into recommendations for participant-centered data sharing.
Our synthesis identified two overarching areas (see Supplementary Table S1): (1) the researcher-participant relationship and (2) data lifecycle governance.

text.text: First, within the researcherparticipant relationship, informed consent should function as a collaborative and communicative agreement between researchers and participants rather than a one-sided authorization.

Researchers should provide complete, accessible, and population-appropriate information, offer meaningful opportunities for questions and clarification, and enable participants to make voluntary decisions about both study participation and the planned sharing of their data.
Second, data lifecycle governance requires informed consent to address how data will be collected, managed, stored, protected, shared, and reused throughout their life cycle.

Participants should understand what information will be collected and shared, how it will be protected, who may access it, how it may be reused, and what withdrawal rights apply. share psychological data and seeking to design a transparent, participant-centered informed consent process.

Four categories of information are particularly important for enabling an informed choice about data sharing: (a) what data sharing entails and why it forms part of the study; (b) which data will be shared and how they will be prepared and protected before dissemination; (c) the conditions governing future access, preservation, licensing, and reuse; and (d) participants' rights, relevant contact points, and any limitations on withdrawal once data have been anonymized or deposited in a repository.
Providing this information reframes informed consent as more than a clause authorizing data disclosure.
Instead, it establishes a transparent agreement concerning the full life cycle of research data and allows openness to become a participant's open choice.
Participants can therefore evaluate both whether they wish to take part in the original study and whether they are willing to authorize the future sharing and reuse of the data they contribute.

Whenever feasible, consent to research participation and consent to future data sharing should be presented as distinguishable choices, so that unspecified secondary use does not become an implicit prerequisite for participation.
Little empirical evidence is available on how psychology journals and researchers have operationalized these principles in the context of open data.

Existing analyses of journal policies have primarily examined general transparency and data-sharing requirements, or the challenges associated with particular forms of data, such as sensitive or stigmatized topics or vulnerable and marginalized populations (i.e., Prosser et al., 2023).

This omission is particularly consequential because the success of Open Science depends not only on researchers' willingness to share data, but also on participants' willingness to contribute their information under conditions that respect their autonomy, rights, and expectations.

The present study addresses this gap by examining how participants' informed consent for future data sharing is currently represented within the psychological domain supporting Open Science.

Because promoting responsible research practices is a shared responsibility of both researchers and the institutions that disseminate scientific knowledge, we examined this issue from two complementary perspectives.
First, we systematically reviewed the data-sharing policies of psychology journals promoting Open Data practices.
Specifically, we investigated whether journal guidelines provide explicit recommendations concerning participants' informed consent for future data sharing.
Second, we examined scholars' reporting practices.

For each selected journal, we first identified recent empirical articles (2024-2025) that openly shared data and then we systematically evaluated the information provided in each article about informed consent.
Particular attention was paid to whether authors reported that participants had been informed that their data could be shared and reused beyond the original study.

By integrating the ethical principles outlined above with the empirical evidence emerging from journal policies and researchers' reporting practices, we also aimed to develop actionable guidelines for researchers, journal editors and publishers, and the scientific community in general, to promote more transparent, participant-centered, and ethically responsible open-data practices.

text.text: None of the 83 reviewed journals provided explicit guidance on consent specifically for sharing participants' data on open platforms.
Four journals referred to consent for secondary use when applicable.
Furthermore, among the 196 articles sharing data we reviewed, only seven (3.57%) connected informed consent to data sharing, usually in repository documents rather than the article itself.
These findings suggest a gap in the transparency extended to participants and in the information available to readers about how data sharing was presented to them.

In the following section we therefore discuss how researchers, journal editors and publishers, and the wider research community can improve both communication with participants about data sharing and the reporting practices.

To facilitate implementation, we developed an informed consent template following indications from Table S1 (available in Supplemental Materials) that provides an adaptable structure for incorporating data-sharing information into the consent process of empirical research involving human participants.

Journal policies can make these expectations explicit.

Although every included journal offered some data-sharing guidance, none directly addressed obtaining participant consent for sharing data on open platforms, and 55 provided no guidance on consent or related ethical issues in the materials examined.

Author instructions should ask researchers to report whether and how prospective data sharing was explained to participants, whether participants were asked to consent to it, and under what conditions the data would be shared and reused.

If consent for sharing was not requested, authors guidelines should request justification and explanation of the circumstances and relevant ethics review or legal basis to be reported in a dedicated section of the manuscript.
For journals awarding Open Data badges, the badge request could include a declaration about whether participants were informed about data sharing and, where relevant, consented to it.
The request should also permit a reasoned explanation in case participant consent for data sharing is not applicable (e.g., non-human participants).

A dedicated badge recognizing clear documentation of how participants were informed and whether they were asked for consent for data sharing could encourage These topics should be taught alongside the technical skills needed to prepare datasets and use repositories.
Together, these measures would support ethical sharing from the design stage rather than only when preparing data for release.
Our review has several limitations.
First, journals were identified through a badge-focused list, and we examined a maximum of three data-sharing articles per journal published online in 2024-2025.
The findings should therefore not be interpreted as prevalence estimates for all psychology journals or articles.
Second, journal policies, repository contents, and linked materials may change over time, meaning that our findings reflect the information available at the time of the review.
Most importantly, our study assessed what was publicly reported, not what necessarily occurred during the original consent process.

The absence of a statement or publicly available consent form does not mean that participants were uninformed, that consent was not obtained, or that researchers lacked an appropriate ethical or legal basis for sharing the data.
Conversely, the presence of a consent statement does not establish that participants fully understood the implications of data sharing or that their consent was freely given.
Future research should therefore examine consent materials directly and investigate participants' understanding, expectations, and experiences of data sharing.
Despite these limitations, our findings identify a clear gap in both journal guidance and research reporting.

As psychological science increasingly promotes the sharing and reuse of research data, transparency should extend not only to researchers who access those data, but also to the participants who make data sharing possible.
Participant-centered data sharing therefore requires that information about future sharing is communicated clearly during the consent process and made visible in the scientific record.

Informed consent is an agreement governing the collection, management, use, storage, and potential sharing of participants' personal data.
Within this agreement, participants should be enabled to understand and actively decide how their personal information may be used throughout the entire research lifecycle.

According to the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), personal data refer to "any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person", either directly or indirectly identifiable through identifiers such as a name, identification number, location data, online identifier, or one or more characteristics specific to that individual's identity (GDPR, Article 4).

Researchers are responsible for collecting only personal data that are strictly necessary to achieve the scientific objectives of the study (data minimization), processing those data in accordance with applicable legal and ethical standards, and clearly informing participants about every stage of the data lifecycle.

This includes explaining which personal data will be collected, why they are needed, how they will be processed and protected, whether they will be shared, and what measures will be implemented to safeguard participants' privacy.

When data sharing is planned, researchers should explicitly distinguish between data collected for the primary research project and data that may subsequently be made available for secondary analyses.

Participants should also be informed about the extent to which researchers can control future access to and reuse of shared datasets and whether participation in the study requires consent to data sharing or whether these represent separate decisions.

This template supports the development of transparent, participant-centered informed consent procedures for psychological research involving human participants and prospective data sharing.
It provides a general structure for communicating study procedures and data-sharing practices.
It is not intended to replace institution-specific privacy notices, legal documentation, ethics requirements, or local regulatory guidance.
Researchers should retain only sections relevant to their study and revise the language to match the characteristics, literacy level, and needs of the target population.
Particular attention should be given to the data-sharing section, which should clearly reflect the actual practices planned for the study rather than generic or hypothetical arrangements.

The legal and data-protection components of this template are intentionally jurisdiction-neutral and should be adapted to the laws, regulations, institutional requirements, and ethics procedures applicable in each context.

text.text: The main finding was that no journal provided explicit guidelines on obtaining such consent.
Nevertheless, 28 of the 83 journals (33.73%) provided some guidance on consent or related ethical issues potentially relevant to data sharing.

In 24 of these journals, this guidance was limited to requiring informed consent under specific circumstances, primarily for the publication of identifiable or personal information, individual-level data, images, videos, or case details.

The remaining four journals (4.82% of the full sample) specified in their guidelines that authors must report in the Method section that informed consent had been obtained from participants, including consent for secondary use of data when applicable.

Although these statements did not explicitly emphasize need to obtain participants' consent specifically for sharing data on open platforms, these journals nevertheless required authors to confirm that participants had consented to future uses of their data, consistent with the APA Ethics Code and the GDPR principles.

Notably, these four journals (Journal of Psychopathology and Clinical Science, Neuropsychology, Psychological Trauma: Theory, Research, Practice, and Policy, and Rehabilitation Psychology) are all published by the American Psychological Association.
Taken together, these findings indicate that, beyond these specific cases, journals rarely provide explicit guidance on obtaining informed consent for data sharing.
